title: Delhi's Six Hours of Blood
subtitle: When Rumour Lit a City and an Empire Bled
era: Nader Shah's sack of Delhi, 1739 CE
moral: Eyewitnesses make denial harder than memory alone.

sources.note: Contemporary Delhi court voice recording local opposition and massacre.

sources.citation: Abdul Karim Khan Kashmiri, Bayan-e-Waqai; Rustam Ali, Tarikh-e-Hindi
sources.note: Contemporary Indo-Persian accounts of the invasion and qatl-i-am.

sources.citation: Michael Axworthy, The Sword of Persia (2006); Jadunath Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire, Vol. 1
sources.note: Modern and classic reconstructions of Nader Shah in India.

panels.shot: high wide shot over Shahjahanabad at dusk, domes and minarets under a looming storm, Nader Shah's troops like dark ants in the streets

dialogue.text: In March 1739, as Nader Shah ruled Delhi for a few days, a rumour, a riot and six hours of slaughter burned a mark no emperor’s pleasure could erase.

panels.shot: slow push-in from a map-like bird’s-eye of North India down to the walled city of Shahjahanabad

dialogue.text: By early 1739, Shahjahanabad still glowed with Mughal splendour, but its armies lay broken. Nader Shah, victor outside Karnal, now camped at its very heart.

panels.shot: medium interior shot in the Diwan-i-Khas, low angle on throne, wide to show Persian presence

dialogue.text: Inside the Red Fort, the Mughal emperor shared his own hall with the Persian conqueror. For now, as Anand Ram Mukhlis notes, Nader demanded obedience, not yet blood.

panels.shot: street-level tracking shot through Chandni Chowk, slightly low angle to show bustle and foreign troops

dialogue.text: Outside, Persian troops quartered in the bazaars and mohallas. They took supplies, demanded payment, and moved in alien silence through lanes that had known only Mughal guards.

panels.shot: intimate interior shot in a small Delhi home, candlelit, faces in half-shadow

dialogue.text: Delhi’s people watched and waited. Some, like Mukhlis, recorded each new insult. Others only clenched their jaws and prayed the storm would pass over their roofs.

panels.shot: dynamic street corner shot, mid-level, capturing first flare of violence

dialogue.text: Tensions grew. Indo-Persian chroniclers speak of quarrels over money and honour, of soldiers taking what they wished in a city that lived on trade and pride.

panels.shot: crowded market square shot, overhead oblique angle, chaos beginning

dialogue.text: Then, as later accounts agree, word raced through the bazaars: Nader Shah is dead. Whether from a scuffle, a misstep or pure rumour, the spark caught dry grass.

panels.shot: fast, kinetic street-level shot with sharp diagonals, conveying erupting fury

dialogue.text: Believing the conqueror fallen, groups of townspeople fell upon isolated Persian bands. Anand Ram notes that in some quarters, Afsharid soldiers were attacked and cut down amidst cries of sudden courage.

panels.shot: wide city-lane shot, slightly elevated, to show scattered skirmishes without graphic detail

dialogue.text: Contemporary estimates speak of thousands of Persian soldiers killed in these sudden clashes. Yet the resistance was scattered, brief, and soon met an answering fury.

panels.shot: interior wide shot in a temporary Persian headquarters, focus on a messenger and Nader Shah

dialogue.text: When news of the killings reached Nader, the tone of his rule in Delhi changed. The chroniclers agree on what followed, though their numbers differ.

panels.shot: exterior wide shot of Sunehri Masjid in Chandni Chowk, slight low angle, massed troops below

dialogue.text: He rode to the Sunehri Masjid in Chandni Chowk. From there, say Abdul Karim and Rustam Ali, the order went out over the crowded square: a general massacre, qatl-i-am.

panels.shot: tight, dramatic close-up on Nader Shah’s raised arm and hard-set face, city blurred behind

dialogue.text: Eyewitnesses describe no long debate, no softening. In his eyes, the killing of his men by Delhi’s people demanded an answer that would not be forgotten.

panels.shot: sweeping overhead shot over a Delhi neighbourhood, soldiers fanning out like a dark flood

dialogue.text: For hours, Persian troops swept through Shahjahanabad’s lanes. Indo-Persian and European reports alike speak of a city where, in many quarters, the invaders met little organised resistance.

panels.shot: mid-level lane shot focusing on civilians’ terror and submission rather than combat

dialogue.text: Mukhlis writes that a few offered opposition, but most were cut down or seized where they stood, unable or unwilling to fight trained soldiers in the maze of their own streets.

panels.shot: interior courtyard shot, intimate, emphasizing loss and fear

dialogue.text: Alongside the killing came seizure. Chroniclers and foreign letters speak of looting and the taking of captives, as houses were forced open and families broken apart.

panels.shot: wide, smoky cityscape shot at a distance, showing fires and stillness after chaos

dialogue.text: By the time Nader called off the slaughter, perhaps tens of thousands lay dead by varying accounts. Delhi’s noise, once of trade and song, fell into a stunned, smoky silence.

panels.shot: somber interior shot of the Diwan-i-Am or a hall in the Red Fort, wide and echoing

dialogue.speaker: muhammad_shah_and_delhi_s_residents
dialogue.text: How does a king answer his people when words come too late?

panels.shot: opulent interior shot of the Peacock Throne being dismantled, focus on artisans and soldiers

dialogue.text: In the days that followed, the qatl-i-am gave way to organised plunder. The Peacock Throne was stripped and carried off, and treasures like the Koh-i-Noor passed into Nader’s possession.

panels.shot: grand riverbank shot of Nader Shah’s camp breaking along the Yamuna, with long columns readying to depart

dialogue.text: Nader Shah also fixed an immense indemnity, forcing Delhi and the court to yield yet more wealth. When his army finally left, it carried away fortunes that had taken generations to build.

panels.shot: quiet, low-angle street shot years later, with repaired but aged buildings, focus on survivors

dialogue.text: For the survivors, Delhi was never the same. Yet life crept back into its lanes, and stories of the six hours when the city bled were passed down with a mixture of grief and hard memory.

panels.shot: extreme close-up on a manuscript page being written, candlelight flickering, hand steady

dialogue.text: Because men like Anand Ram Mukhlis and Abdul Karim wrote what they saw and heard, Delhi’s six hours of blood cannot be wished away. Their ink keeps both resistance and ruin from fading into legend.
